title: The Turnip
paragraphs: Two brothers were both soldiers, one rich and one poor. The poor one decided to try to improve his lot, so he took off his red coat, became a gardener, dug his plot thoroughly, and planted turnips.

When the seeds sprouted, one plant grew bigger than all the others. It kept on growing and growing and seemed as though it would never stop, so that it could have been called the prince of turnips, since there had never been one like it before and never would be again. In the end it was so big that it filled a whole cart, and two oxen could barely pull it. The gardener had no idea what to do with it, or whether it would turn out to be a blessing or a curse for him. One day he said to himself, ‘What am I going to do with it? If I sell it, it will fetch no more than any other turnip, and for eating, the small ones are better. Perhaps the best thing is to take it to the king as a token of respect.’

So he yoked his oxen, hauled the turnip to the court, and presented it to the king. ‘What an amazing thing!’ said the king. ‘I have seen many strange things, but never a monster like this. Where did you get the seed? Or is it just your good luck? If so, you are a true child of fortune.’ ‘Oh, no,’ answered the gardener, ‘I am no child of fortune. I am a poor soldier who could never get enough to live on, so I put away my red coat and went to work on the land. I have a brother who is rich. Your majesty knows him well, and so does everyone else. But because I am poor, everybody forgets me.’

The king felt sorry for him and said, ‘You shall be poor no longer. I will give you so much that you will be even richer than your brother.’ Then he gave him gold, land and livestock, and made him so wealthy that his brother’s fortune could not begin to compare with his.

When the brother heard about all this, and how a turnip had made the gardener rich, he was bitterly jealous and began to think how he could win the same good fortune for himself. He decided, though, to go about it more cleverly than his brother. He collected a rich present of gold and fine horses for the king, and expected to receive a much bigger gift in return. After all, if his brother had been given so much for just a turnip, what would his own present be worth?

The king accepted the gift graciously and said he had nothing more valuable and wonderful to give in return than the great turnip. So the soldier had to load it onto a cart and drag it home. When he got there, he did not know whom to take his rage and spite out on, until finally wicked thoughts came into his head, and he decided to kill his brother.

He hired some villains to murder him, showed them where to hide in ambush, and then went to his brother and said, ‘Dear brother, I have found a hidden treasure. Let’s go and dig it up and split it between us.’ The other suspected no treachery, so they set off together. As they were walking along, the murderers leapt out at him, tied him up, and were about to hang him from a tree.

But while they were making everything ready, they heard a horse trampling in the distance, which scared them so much that they shoved their prisoner into a sack, head and shoulders together, hoisted him up to the tree with a cord, left him dangling there, and ran off. Meanwhile he worked and worked away at the sack until he had made a hole big enough to stick his head out.

The rider turned out to be a student, a cheerful fellow, traveling along on his horse and singing as he went. As soon as the man in the sack saw him passing under the tree, he called out, ‘Good morning! Good morning to you, my friend!’ The student looked all around, and seeing no one, and not knowing where the voice was coming from, called back, ‘Who is calling me?’

Then the man in the tree answered, ‘Raise your eyes, for here I sit in the sack of wisdom. In a short time I have learned great and wonderful things here. Compared with this seat, all the learning of the schools is empty air. A little longer, and I shall know everything a man can know, and I shall come out wiser than the wisest of mankind. Here I can read the signs and movements of the heavens and the stars, the laws that rule the winds, the number of the grains of sand on the seashore, the healing of the sick, and the powers of all herbs, birds and precious stones. If you were here for just a moment, my friend, you would feel and admit the power of knowledge.’

The student listened to all this in amazement. At last he said, ‘Blessed be the day and hour when I found you! Can’t you find a way to let me into the sack for a little while?’ The other answered, as though very reluctant, ‘I might let you sit here for a short time, if you reward me well and treat me kindly. But you must wait an hour down there, until I have learned a few small things that I still don’t know.’

So the student sat down and waited a while, but the time dragged, and he begged earnestly to go up at once, for his thirst for knowledge was great. Then the other pretended to give in and said, ‘You must let the sack of wisdom down by untying that cord over there, and then you may get in.’ So the student let him down, opened the sack, and set him free. ‘Now then,’ he cried, ‘let me up quickly!’ As he began to climb into the sack feet first, ‘Wait a moment,’ said the gardener, ‘that is not the way.’ Then he pushed him in head first, tied up the sack, and soon had the seeker after wisdom swinging in the air. ‘How are you, friend?’ he said. ‘Don’t you feel wisdom coming to you? Rest there in peace until you are wiser than you were.’
With that, he rode off on the student’s horse and left the poor fellow to gather wisdom until somebody came along and let him down.
